1:
The parable of the labourers in the vineyard divides the cloud of witnesses along a clear fault-line: the fathers read it as a sweeping allegory of salvation-history, while the modern and Reformed commentators rein it in to its one stated point — that ‘the last shall be first’ (v.16).

The Latin and Greek fathers mine every detail. Gregory the Great and Pseudo-Chrysostom read the hours as the ages of the world — morning (Adam to Noah), the third, sixth and ninth hours (Noah, Abraham, Moses), the eleventh the coming of Christ and the call of the Gentiles — or, alternatively, as the stages of human life from childhood to decrepit old age. Remigius, Jerome and the Gloss take the householder as Christ (or the Father working through the Son), the vineyard as the Church, the denarius as the reward of eternal life stamped, like a coin, with the King’s image. Origen (Alexandrian) calls the whole present life one day and the marketplace all that lies outside the Church. Augustine adds the refinement that, though all receive the one denarius of eternal life, ‘there are with the Father many mansions’ (compare John 14:2), so that one shines more than another.

The grammatical-historical commentators supply the framework and resist excess. Barnes insists the kingdom ‘has reference to rewards,’ and ties the vineyard to Isaiah 5:7 and Jeremiah 12:10. Ellicott laments the chapter division and roots the parable in the preceding story of the rich young ruler and the disciples’ ‘What shall we have?’ (Matthew 19:27), reading the householder as Christ and the labourers as the ‘hired servants’ of Luke 15:17. Robertson notes the classic idiom for break of day.

The Reformed Calvin sharply curbs the allegory: the parable is only a confirmation of the saying that the first have ‘no right to boast or to insult others,’ for God may call latecomers and make them equal; to ‘sift out with exactness every portion’ is ‘useless curiosity.’ The Puritan Henry and Wesleyan Wesley hold both senses together — the rejection of the Jews and call of the Gentiles, and the general truth that God is debtor to no man.
2:
‘He agreed with the labourers for a penny a day.’ The verse turns on the coin and on the contract, and the grammatical-historical commentators take up both.

The ‘penny’ is the Roman denarius. Albert Barnes traces the name to its first value, ten brass asses, ‘whence its name,’ and describes the coin itself: the consular denarius carried a head of Rome on one side with an X or a star to mark its worth in asses, and a chariot of two or four horses; later the casts of the deities gave way, on the obverse, to the heads of the Caesars. Adam Clarke reckons it ‘equal to the Greek drachma,’ and both he and Barnes put its sterling value at about sevenpence-halfpenny, the ordinary price of a day’s labour and the standing wage of a Roman soldier (Matthew 18:28). Charles Ellicott warns that weight is the wrong measure: the coin’s ‘real equivalent… is to be found in its purchasing power,’ which, as the average hire of a tiller of the soil, he reckons ‘equal to about half-a-crown of our present currency’ — ‘in itself, an adequate and just payment.’ A.T. Robertson likewise prefers ‘shilling’ to ‘penny.’

John Lightfoot brings the rabbinic canons to bear. He sets the silver penny against the gold, which exceeded it twenty-four times, a penny of gold being worth ‘five-and-twenty of silver’; then he observes that the Hebrew rules on hiring distinguish, ‘as reason requires, between being hired by the day, and being hired (only) for some hours.’ The parable keeps the same distinction: the morning men are engaged for the whole day and for a penny, the later ones for certain hours, with ‘a part of a penny allotted them, in proportion to the time they wrought.’ The Reformed John Gill places the first labourers in that same rabbinic class, those ‘hired for a day.’ This, Lightfoot thinks, is why a fixed sum is named only with the first.

Clarke cannot resist his own country’s past, where in 1351 parliament fixed the wages of ‘corn-weeders and hay-makers, without meat, drink, or other courtesy demanded,’ at a penny a day, and in 1314 a chaplain to the Scotch bishops, then prisoners in England, was allowed three halfpence. Barnes adds that provisions were cheap in proportion, so that what the labourer’s penny bought him in food was nearly what a day’s wage buys now. The wage of the parable is therefore neither mean nor lavish but the just hire of one day; and it is precisely because the first labourers struck that bargain freely that their murmuring, when it comes, will have nothing to stand on.
3:
‘He went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace.’ The hour and the scene are quickly fixed; what the idleness signifies is not.

The grammatical-historical commentators settle the time and place. Gill, Barnes and Clarke explain that the Jews divided the day into twelve hours from sunrise, so the third hour was about nine in the morning. Barnes notes the marketplace was where provisions were sold and where, therefore, employers and the unemployed would naturally meet — the idle were ‘not disposed to be idle, but were waiting in the proper place to find employers.’ Robertson cites a traveller’s account of peasants gathering before sunrise at Hamadan in Persia, ‘with spades in their hands, waiting to be hired for the day.’

Ellicott, reckoning the Jewish day from six in the morning, brings the third hour to about eight, and presses the spiritual meaning: in the labourers called after the first he sees a reference to those summoned later, like Matthew (Matthew 9:9) and the disciples called in Matthew 8:19-22, after the sons of Jonas and Zebedee. Thus the staggered calls picture the successive summons of men into the kingdom.

The Puritan Matthew Henry reads the idleness morally, and so takes it the other way from Barnes. Asked whence the labourers are hired, he answers: out of the market-place, ‘where, till they are hired into God’s service, they stand idle’ — and all the day idle (v.6). The soul of man ‘stands ready to be hired into some service or other’; it was created to work, and is ‘either a servant to iniquity, or a servant to righteousness’ (Romans 6:19). The devil is hiring as well, ‘into his field, to feed swine,’ while God by his gospel hires ‘into his vineyard, to dress it, and keep it, paradise-work.’ On this reading a sinful state, ‘though a state of drudgery to Satan, may really be called a state of idleness’: sinners are busy enough, but doing ‘nothing that will pass well in the account.’ Henry hears a rebuke in the place itself. The market-place is one of concourse, where Wisdom cries (Proverbs 1:20-21); a place of sport, where the children are playing (Matthew 11:16); a place of business, ‘of noise and hurry’; and the gospel calls men out of all three — ‘Come, come from this market-place.’ Where Barnes finds willing men waiting in the right spot, Henry finds the world loitering in the wrong one.
4:
‘Go ye also into the vineyard, and whatsoever is right I will give you.’ The absence of a fixed wage, and the trust it implies, is what the commentators fasten on.

The grammatical-historical commentators draw out the change of terms. Barnes notes that the contract with the first was definite, but with these it ‘depended on the judgment of the employer’ — ‘whatsoever it shall appear you can earn.’ Robertson parses the clause as an indefinite relative with the subjunctive, and glosses it ‘a just proportionate wage,’ not whatever the householder pleased. Ellicott presses the spiritual point hardest: the absence of a definite contract ‘involved an implicit trust in the equity of the householder.’ These labourers did not stipulate for wages, nor ask, as the disciples had asked, ‘What shall we have therefore?’ (Matthew 19:27); and the lesson implied is that ‘a little work done, when God calls us, in the spirit of trust, is better than much done in the spirit of a hireling.’

The Reformed Gill reads the call typologically as ‘a call of divine grace out of the world into the church,’ arising from mere goodwill without any merit in man: the householder goes out to these men, not they to him; he questions and calls and bids them go, while ‘they do not ask him to hire them.’ The persons called, Gill notes, are ‘a parcel of idle, mean, vulgar people… the weak, base, and foolish things of the world’ (compare 1 Corinthians 1:27).

The Puritan Matthew Henry takes up both halves of the summons. The work first: the church is God’s vineyard, ‘of his planting, watering, and fencing,’ and the religion men are hired for is ‘vineyard-work, pruning, dressing, digging, watering, fencing, weeding.’ Each has his own plot in it — ‘our own soul; and it is God’s and to be kept and dressed for him’ — so that the hired must be ‘not slothful, not loiterers, but labourers’: ‘a man may go idle to hell; but he that will go to heaven, must be busy.’ Then the wages. Henry refers the promise of ‘whatsoever is right’ to this verse and the three that follow, and reads it as a guarantee rather than a vagueness: ‘God will be sure not to be behind-hand with any for the service they do him: never any lost by working for God.’ What is held out is ‘a crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge shall give.’ The open term, then, is not a weaker offer than the fixed penny but a better one, and those who take it without haggling stand nearest the parable’s own temper.
5:
‘Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise.’ The comment divides between the timekeeping and the typology.

The Wesleyan Adam Clarke supplies the bare reckoning: the sixth hour was twelve o’clock, the ninth three in the afternoon — the fixed points of the working day at which the householder went out yet again to seek labourers.

The Reformed Gill adds a devotional observation: those named seasons were also the Jewish hours of prayer, and the householder, ‘seeing others in the same place, and posture… called them, and sent them into his vineyard, to labour there, giving them the same promise he did to others.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry puts these middle calls to work twice over. In the history of the gospel, the apostles went out first while Christ was on earth, on a first and a second mission, their business then being to call in the Jews; after the ascension they went again on the same errand, preaching to Jews only, in Judea first and afterwards to those of the dispersion; and not until ‘as it were about the eleventh hour’ did they summon the Gentiles to the same work and privilege, telling them that in Christ Jesus no difference should be made between Jew and Greek. Read instead of a single life, the same seasons become the conversion of men already settled in their ways. Divine grace, Henry says, ‘is magnified in the conversion of some, when they are in the midst of their pleasures and worldly pursuits, as Paul.’ God ‘has work for all ages; no time amiss to turn to God,’ and he ‘turns away none that are willing to be hired, for yet there is room.’

Henry distinguishes the two callings that the repeated journeys imply: ‘the common call is promiscuous, to come and work in the vineyard; but the effectual call is particular, and it is then effectual when we come at the call.’ What the verse adds to the parable, then, is that the summons is not given once at daybreak and done with. The promise of ‘whatsoever is right’ (v.4) attends every fresh going-out, and the householder keeps returning to the same spot while any part of the day remains.
6:
‘About the eleventh hour he found others standing idle… Why stand ye here all the day idle?’ The lateness of the hour, and what the last call means, is the question.

The grammatical-historical commentators fix the time and probe the idleness. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree the eleventh hour was about five in the afternoon, with only one working hour left before the day closed at six (compare John 11:9). Robertson, parsing the accusative of time, names this bluntly ‘the problem of the unemployed,’ the word for idle being ‘no work.’ Ellicott detects a sharper edge: there was still urgent work to be done, the first labourers ‘were not enough,’ and perhaps ‘not labouring as zealously as they might,’ working merely on contract, while those called last had the joy of feeling their day was not lost.

The Reformed Gill reads the hours typologically as either the ages of the world (before the law, under the law, the Messiah’s times, the last days), or the dispensations of the gospel, or the stages of human life — childhood, youth, manhood, and old age — the eleventh hour standing for those called in old age and, ultimately, the Gentiles (compare Hebrews 6:12). Wesley adds simply that the eleventh hour means ‘very late, long after the rest were called.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry takes the old-age reading and presses it both ways. Some are hired ‘in old age, at the eleventh hour, when the day of life is far spent, and there is but one hour of the twelve remaining’; but ‘none are hired at the twelfth hour; when life is done, opportunity is done.’ Within that limit he finds two grounds of hope. There is hope for old sinners, since ‘if, in sincerity, they turn to God, they shall doubtless be accepted; true repentance is never too late.’ And there is hope of them, that they may be brought to repentance at all: ‘nothing is too hard for Almighty grace to do, it can change the Ethiopian’s skin, and the leopard’s spots; can set those to work, who have contracted a habit of idleness.’ Nicodemus, he notes, ‘may be born again when he is old.’ Then the warning: ‘yet let none, upon this presumption, put off their repentance till they are old.’ So the eleventh hour is a door, not a plan — and the question that opens the verse is less rebuke than summons, drawing the last labourers in while a moment of the day remains.
7:
‘Because no man hath hired us… Go ye also into the vineyard.’ The latecomers’ excuse is taken as genuine, and their obedience as prompt.

The grammatical-historical commentators take the plea at face value. Ellicott calls this ‘one of the salient points of the parable’: the last-called labourers ‘had not rejected any previous summons, and when called they obeyed with alacrity… in full unquestioning faith.’ Barnes cross-refers to the urgency of working while opportunity lasts (John 9:4, Ecclesiastes 9:10). Clarke notes that ‘no man hath hired us’ was the very reason they had stood idle, and observes that the clause ‘whatsoever is right, that shall ye receive’ is wanting in some of the best manuscripts.

The Reformed Gill applies the excuse pointedly to the Gentiles, who for ‘hundreds of years were neglected by God’ — he ‘overlooked the times of their ignorance’ and ‘sent no prophets to instruct them’ — until, the Jews having rejected the Messiah and his apostles, the gospel was ordered to the nations.

The Puritan Matthew Henry agrees that the plea is honest, and then takes away the comfort most readers draw from it. These men came at the eleventh hour, ‘but nobody had hired them, or offered to hire them, before’; the Gentiles likewise came in late ‘because the gospel had not been before preached to them.’ The excuse, that is, belongs only to the unsummoned. ‘Those that have had gospel offers made them at the third, or sixth hour, and have resisted and refused them, will not have that to say for themselves at the eleventh hour, that these had; No man has hired us.’ Nor, Henry adds, can such presume on a later call: they cannot ‘be sure that any man will hire them at the ninth or eleventh hour.’ The conclusion is not discouragement but urgency — ‘not to discourage any, but to awaken all, be it remembered, that now is the accepted time; if we will hear his voice, it must be to-day.’

So the idleness of the last labourers was no fault of theirs, and they came the moment they were summoned; which both heightens the equity of a householder who rewards willing latecomers in full, and leaves the man who has already refused a call with nothing of their defence to plead.
8:
‘When even was come… beginning from the last unto the first.’ The order of payment, and the just custom of paying at day’s end, are what the commentators weigh — and they do not agree about how much the order means.

The grammatical-historical commentators explain the scene. Barnes describes the steward as the trusted servant who managed the household and paid the workers, and notes that the order — last to first — was immaterial to justice but essential to the parable, for ‘had those first hired been first paid, they would have departed satisfied, and the point… would have been lost.’ Lightfoot and Ellicott ground the prompt payment in the humane Mosaic law that the day-labourer must be paid the same day (Deuteronomy 24:15); the householder’s keeping of it is ‘a feature in his character.’ Ellicott adds that the order illustrates the saying that ‘the last should be first.’

The Reformed Calvin checks the allegorisers: ‘it would be improper to look for a mystery in the injunction’ as if God crowned first those last in time, ‘for such a notion would not at all agree with the doctrine of Paul’ (1 Thessalonians 4:15). The order serves only to make the murmuring possible, and so to teach that men have ‘no right to complain of the bounty of God’ when he honours the unworthy with rewards beyond their deserving.

The Puritan Matthew Henry goes exactly where Calvin forbids, and to the same text. He first reads the hour: ‘evening time is the reckoning time; the particular account must be given up in the evening of our life; for after death cometh the judgment,’ God keeping his own rule that the hire shall not ‘abide with thee all night.’ So ‘ministers call them into the vineyard, to do their work; death calls them out of the vineyard, to receive their penny: and those to whom the call into the vineyard is effectual, the call out of it will be joyful.’ Then he presses the sequence itself: the last are called first ‘lest they should be discouraged,’ and at the great day, ‘though the dead in Christ shall rise first, yet they which are alive and remain… shall be caught up together with them in the clouds; no preference shall be given to seniority.’ Where Calvin cites Paul to rule the reading out, Henry cites the same chapter to let it in; and between them the verse is left either a plain stroke of narrative craft or a picture of the last day, with its promptness and its justice admitted on both sides.
9:
‘They that were hired about the eleventh hour… received every man a penny.’ The full wage to the one-hour men is the parable’s great surprise.

The grammatical-historical commentators stress the equity in the generosity. Barnes notes there was ‘no agreement how much they should receive, but merely that justice should be done’ (v.4), and that the householder either reckoned they had earned it or chose ‘to make a present… for the loss of the first part of the day.’ Ellicott presses that the idleness was no fault of theirs, and their readiness at the eleventh hour implied they would have come as readily at daybreak; so ‘the standard of payment was qualitative, not quantitative,’ and the penny represents the eternal life of the kingdom — ‘no true labourer could receive less; the longest life of labour could claim no more’ (compare Luke 23:40-43).

The Reformed Gill reads the eleventh-hour men as those called in old age, or as the Gentiles, or as the last of the elect called at the end of the world. The Wesleyan Wesley holds both senses open: they are ‘either the Gentiles, who were called long after the Jews… or those in every age who did not hear, or at least understand, the Gospel call, till their day of life was drawing to a period.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry supplies the arithmetic of grace, and then turns it on the reader. The whole wage for a tenth of the work ‘is designed to show that God distributes his rewards by grace and sovereignty, and not of debt’; what is obtained is eternal life, ‘not as wages for the value of their work, but as the gift of God.’ Degrees of glory he grants, but no shortfall: ‘in heaven, every vessel will be full, brimful, though every vessel is not alike large and capacious,’ and in the sharing of future joys, as in the gathering of the manna, ‘he that shall gather much, will have nothing over, and he that shall gather little, will have no lack’ (Exodus 16:18). Those who come in late, ‘picked up out of the highways and the hedges,’ sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the same feast. Then the sting: the best of the labourers, with ‘so many empty spaces in their time,’ may truly be said to have laboured ‘scarcely one hour of their twelve,’ so that the first are themselves eleventh-hour men, and their defective service is ‘not only… accepted, but by free grace richly rewarded.’
10:
‘When the first came, they supposed that they should have received more.’ The false expectation is the seedbed of the grumbling, and several commentators see the Jews’ claim to precedence in it.

The grammatical-historical commentators trace the disappointed hope. Barnes notes they expected payment ‘not according to contract, but according to the time of the labour.’ Robertson, with Bruce’s wit, asks whether the householder was a humorist in paying each the agreed denarius: ‘false hopes had been raised in those who came first.’ Ellicott turns the lens on the disciples: now, ‘unless they were altogether blind, they must have seen their own thoughts reflected in the parable’ — they too, as their question showed (Matthew 19:27), had expected to receive more, thinking eternal life not enough without ‘some special prerogative.’ Yet the paying of their wage ‘gives a touch of gentleness,’ as with the elder son who was told all the father had was his (Luke 15:31).

The Reformed Gill and the Wesleyan Wesley apply it to the Jews: Gill reads the first as ‘the first saints… or the Jews that first believed,’ and Wesley says plainly ‘the first here may mean the Jews, who supposed they should always be preferred before the Gentiles.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry diagnoses the miscalculation as a standing human habit: ‘there is a great proneness in us to think that we have too little, and other too much, of the tokens of God’s favour; and that we do too much, and others too little, in the work of God.’ We are all ‘very apt… to undervalue the deserts of others, and to overvalue our own.’ He then names the man in the room. Perhaps, he suggests, Christ is giving an intimation to Peter, ‘not to boast too much, as he seemed to do, of his having left all to follow Christ; as if, because he and the rest of them had borne the burthen and heat of the day thus, they must have a heaven by themselves.’ It is hard, Henry allows, ‘for those that do or suffer more than ordinary for God, not to be elevated too much with the thought of it, and to expect to merit by it’ — and he sets Paul against them, who, ‘though the chief of the apostles… owned himself to be nothing, to be less than the least of all saints.’ The disappointment, then, is not an accusation against the householder but a mirror held up to the men who carry it.
11:
‘They murmured against the goodman of the house.’ The grumbling is the parable’s turning-point, and most of the commentators read it as the Jews’ resentment of the Gentiles’ admission.

The grammatical-historical commentators handle word and sense. Barnes and Ellicott both correct the rendering ‘goodman of the house’ to ‘householder,’ the same word as in v.1, an ‘archaic English phrase’ needlessly varied. Robertson notes the verb is onomatopoetic — ‘murmur and grumble are similar’ — and probably an inchoative imperfect, ‘began to grumble,’ found in old Ionic and the papyri. Ellicott marks the Greek tense as ‘repeated and prolonged murmurs.’

The Wesleyan Clarke gives the historical application: the Jews ‘made the preaching of the Gospel to the Gentiles a pretense why they should reject that Gospel,’ imagining themselves the sole objects of the divine approbation, and he points to their murmuring in Acts 11:1 and Acts 15:1. He notes that many such similitudes circulated among the Jews, but that the Lord ‘greatly improved’ them. Gill reads the murmurers as receiving only ‘the external privileges of the Gospel dispensation.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry enters a caution the others pass over. The murmuring cannot be read as happening in heaven: ‘there is, or can be, [no] discontent or murmuring in heaven, for that is both guilt and grief, and in heaven there is neither.’ What the parable pictures is discontent ‘concerning heaven and heavenly things, while they are in prospect and promise in this world’ — a quarrel carried on here about what is promised there. With Clarke he takes the grumbling to signify ‘the jealousy which the Jews were provoked to by the admission of the Gentiles into the kingdom of heaven,’ and he supplies the parallel that fixes the temper exactly: as the elder brother ‘repined at the reception of his younger brother, and complained of his father’s generosity to him, so these labourers quarrelled with their master, and found fault, not because they had not enough, so much as because others were made equal with them.’ That distinction is the whole of it. The complaint is not of short pay but of shared pay, which is the disposition v.15 will name the ‘evil eye’; and the next verse gives it its sharpest and most plausible voice.
12:
‘These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day.’ The grievance is plausible, and most of the commentators press its application to the Jews.

The grammatical-historical commentators bring the scene to life. Barnes explains the ‘burden and heat of the day’ as the severe toil borne through the heat, while the latecomers worked ‘in the cool of the evening.’ Ellicott and Robertson identify the ‘heat’ with the kauson, the scorching east wind or sirocco that ‘blasted the grain in Pharaoh’s dream’ (Genesis 41:6), ‘withered Jonah’s gourd’ (Jonah 4:8), and blighted the vine in Ezekiel’s parable (Ezekiel 17:10); Robertson grants the sweat-stained men ‘seemed to have a good case.’

The Reformed Gill and the Wesleyan Wesley press the application to the Jews. Gill notes the grievance that one hour’s service should be paid as many hours’, ‘grudged by the Jews.’ Wesley turns it directly to Acts 15:9: ‘Thou hast made them equal to us’ — God ‘hath put no difference between us (Jews) and them (Gentiles), purifying their hearts by faith’; and those ‘equally holy here… will be equally happy hereafter.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry hears the words as a boast and measures it. The labourers plead their service ‘as the prodigal’s elder brother did’; and the burden and heat of the day ‘was the most they could make of it’ — the whole of their case stated at its strongest. Against that he sets a comparison that shrinks it: sinners are said to labour ‘in the very fire’ (Habakkuk 2:13), whereas God’s servants ‘at the worst, do but labour in the sun; not in the heat of the iron furnace, but only in the heat of the day.’ Nor does he let the Jewish application stay abstract: the Gentiles newly called in ‘have as much of the privileges of the kingdom of the Messiah as the Jews have, who have so long been labouring in the vineyard of the Old-Testament church, under the yoke of the ceremonial law, in expectation of that kingdom.’ The complaint, in other words, is not that the wage was short but that the hours were counted at all — and the householder’s reply will take up that premise and refuse it.
13:
‘Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?’ The reply rests on strict justice, and the commentators divide over the tone of the word ‘friend.’

The grammatical-historical commentators hear a rebuke in the address. Ellicott and Robertson note that ‘friend’ (literally comrade) ‘always carries with it in our Lord’s lips a tone of reproof,’ used also to the man without a wedding garment (Matthew 22:12) and to Judas (Matthew 26:50). Barnes draws the lesson that the householder, having fully met the contract, may do as he pleases with the rest — so Christians who are just and pay their debts ‘have a right to do with it as they please,’ giving to the poor or to missions. Ellicott adds that, had the first labourers shared the householder’s generosity, ‘they would not have grudged the others’ but found their reward in sympathy, as no disciple entered into his Master’s spirit would grudge the penitent thief his rest in Paradise (Luke 23:43).

The Wesleyan Clarke applies it to the call of the Gentiles, which ‘can in itself become no impediment to the Jews… there is room enough in heaven for all.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry takes the address the opposite way, as courtesy rather than reproof: ‘he calls him friend, for in reasoning with others we should use soft words and hard arguments; if our inferiors are peevish and provoking, yet we should not thereby be put into a passion, but speak calmly to them.’ The hard argument is then the bargain. Behind it Henry sets the axiom that ‘God can do no wrong,’ which is ‘the prerogative of the King of kings’ (Romans 3:5-6), and draws the double consequence: ‘because it is free grace, that is given to those that have it, boasting is for ever excluded; and because it is free grace, that is withheld from those that have it not, murmuring is for ever excluded.’ He presses the appeal to the contract home on the reader, since ‘it is good for us often to consider what it was that we agreed with God for’: carnal worldlings ‘agree with God for their penny in this world… and with these they shall be put off’ — they have what they chose, and in that ‘God does them no wrong’ — while obedient believers agree ‘for their penny in the other world,’ and must remember that they have so agreed.
14:
‘Take that thine is, and go thy way: I will give unto this last, even as unto thee.’ The words are at once a dismissal and a declaration of sovereign generosity, and what the dismissal means for the murmurer is disputed.

The grammatical-historical commentators handle tone and difficulty. Barnes reads it simply: ‘Take what is justly due to you — what is properly your own’ (compare John 17:2). Robertson catches the manner: ‘pick it up,’ as if the man had ‘contemptuously thrown the denarius on the ground,’ and locates the point of the parable in the householder’s sovereign ‘what I will… in the sphere of my own affairs.’ Ellicott raises the harder question — whether the murmuring labourers, though paid, are by their discontent ‘excluded… from all share’ in the reward — and answers that the reward ‘lies in the presence of God to the soul,’ whose blessedness depends on harmony with the mind of God, so that heaven ‘is not a place, but a state.’

The Reformed Gill reads the dismissal as true of ‘many among the Jews, who were only nominal professors, and from whom the Gospel… was taken.’ The Wesleyan Wesley hears the householder’s sovereign will to give ‘to this last called among the heathens even as to the first called among the Jews,’ and even to ‘the late converted publicans and sinners.’

The Puritan Matthew Henry finds the sentence cuts two ways depending on what ‘thine’ is taken to mean. Taken of what belongs to us ‘by debt or absolute propriety, it would be a dreadful word; we are all undone, if we be put off with that only which we can call our own’ — indeed the highest creature ‘must go away into nothing’ if nothing but his desert goes with him. Taken of what comes by gift, ‘the free gift of God, it teaches us to be content with such things as we have’: ‘instead of repining that we have no more, let us take what we have, and be thankful.’ If God is kinder elsewhere, no ground of complaint remains ‘while he is so much better to us than we deserve, in giving us our penny, though we are unprofitable servants.’ On the second half Henry hears a settled resolve rather than a concession — ‘I am resolved I will’ — and takes the unchangeableness of God’s purposes to be itself the silencing of the murmur: ‘he is in one mind, and who can turn him? Neither giveth he an account of any of his matters.’
15:
‘Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?’ Two themes meet here: the householder’s sovereignty and the nature of envy.

The grammatical-historical commentators expound the ‘evil eye.’ Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree the Hebrew idiom denotes the envious and malicious (Deuteronomy 15:9, Proverbs 23:6), ‘displeased at the prosperity of others’ (compare Mark 7:22); Robertson contrasts the grudging eye with the householder’s generous one. Ellicott stresses that the question ‘appeals tacitly to a standard which none could question’: as far as the labourer was concerned, the householder had a right to give freely of his own, being ‘responsible to God only.’

The Reformed Gill reads the ‘mine own’ as the external gifts, the special grace, and the heaven that are God’s to bestow on whom he will — chosen, adopted, justified and glorified ‘according to his sovereign good will and pleasure’ (compare Romans 9:15-24). The Wesleyan Wesley sets a firm limit: from a right to give the undeserving more than they merit it cannot be inferred that God may ‘consign an unborn soul to hell’; the sovereignty is one of bounty, and the question about the eye rebukes a selfish and envious temper.

The Puritan Matthew Henry sharpens the sovereignty by a distinction the others pass over: ‘what we have, is not our own, and therefore it is not lawful for us to do what we will with it; but what God has, is his own.’ That justifies him in providence as in grace — when he takes away what we could ill spare, abstulit, sed et dedit, ‘he hath taken away; but he originally gave’ — and leaves us ‘as clay in the hands of a potter.’ On the second question Henry anatomises envy. It is an evil eye, and ‘the eye is often both the inlet and the outlet of this sin’: Saul saw David prosper ‘and he eyed him’ (1 Samuel 18:9). It is ‘displeased at the good of others, and desires their hurt’ — ‘grief to ourselves, anger to God, and ill-will to our neighbour’ — and it is a sin ‘that has neither pleasure, profit, nor honour, in it; it is an evil, an only evil.’ Its aggravation lies in the clause that names it: envy is ‘unlikeness to God, who is good, and doeth good, and delighteth in doing good,’ and so breaks both great commandments at once, love to God ‘in whose will we should acquiesce’ and love to the neighbour ‘in whose welfare we should rejoice.’ Thus, Henry concludes, ‘man’s badness takes occasion from God’s goodness to be more exceedingly sinful.’
16:
‘So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.’ This is the parable’s moral, and the commentators divide sharply over its reach.

The grammatical-historical commentators narrow it. Barnes argues the parable ‘teaches one truth, and but one’: that within the church Christ makes a difference, raising some (Paul, Martyn, Brainerd) to wider usefulness and higher reward ‘without regard to the time which they serve’ — it has ‘no reference to the call of the Gentiles… nor to the doctrine of election.’ Robertson notes the adjectives change places from Matthew 19:30, suiting the parable. Ellicott reads it of degrees in the life to come, depending ‘not on the duration of service… but on the temper and character of the worker,’ with a latent reference to the rich young ruler; he and Clarke both note that ‘many… few chosen’ is absent from the best manuscripts here (it stands in Matthew 22:14).

The Reformed Calvin likewise restrains it: Christ does not here compare Jew and Gentile or reprobate and elect, but only urges that whoever is called before others should ‘run with so much the greater alacrity’ and share the common prize modestly, since God ‘calls freely whomsoever He pleases.’ The Wesleyan Clarke and Wesley keep the Jew/Gentile sense, Clarke illustrating the ‘many called, few chosen’ by the Roman custom of selecting soldiers; Wesley glosses ‘called’ as all who hear the gospel, ‘chosen’ as only those who obey it.

The Puritan Matthew Henry adds a reach none of the others allows: a future one. The Jewish converts who seemed to have the start of others ‘might possibly be outstripped by their successors in profession,’ for the Gentile church, ‘as yet unborn,’ the Gentile world that ‘as yet stood idle in the market-place,’ would yield ‘greater numbers of eminent, useful Christians’ than were found among the Jews. Nor does he stop at the first century: ‘who knows but that the church, in its old age, may be more fat and flourishing than ever’? What labourers may be sent in ‘in the eleventh hour of the church’s day… and what plentiful effusions of the Spirit may then be, above what has been yet, who can tell?’ On the disputed second clause he takes the opposite line from Ellicott and Clarke, pressing rather than discounting it: ‘many are called with a common call, that are not chosen with a saving choice,’ and so it ‘highly concerns us to build our hope for heaven upon the rock of an eternal choice, and not upon the sand of an external call’ (compare 2 Peter 1:10).
17:
Jesus, going up to Jerusalem, takes the twelve apart to foretell his passion. This is the third and fullest prediction of the cross, and the privacy of it is what most of the commentators dwell on.

The Greek and Latin fathers probe the manner. Chrysostom explains why the disclosure is private: ‘it was not meet that his discourse about these things should be published to the many,’ for if the disciples were confounded, much more the multitude; he stresses that Jesus comes to his passion ‘wittingly and willingly.’ Pseudo-Chrysostom adds that ‘the more precious treasure is ever committed to the more worthy vessels,’ and that to be willing to die ‘is more than human.’ Jerome and Raban note he fortifies them against the scandal of the cross, Raban tracing the chain — Judas to the Jews, the Jews to the Gentiles. Augustine draws from the two deaths and one resurrection a meditation on the number three.

The grammatical-historical commentators and the Reformed Calvin add the setting and the purpose. Barnes and Ellicott place the journey after the raising of Lazarus and the sojourn at Ephraim (John 11:54), and note from Mark that Jesus ‘went before them’ while they ‘were amazed… and afraid’ (Mark 10:32) — the shadow of the cross already upon him. Calvin says he repeats the prediction to ‘exhort them to steadiness,’ fortifying them by foreknowledge and by the proof of his divinity.

The Puritan Henry works the privacy out furthest. Jerusalem had to be the scene twice over: there the passover must be kept (Deuteronomy 12:5), and there ‘a prophet must perish, because there the great Sanhedrim sat, who were judges in that case’ (Luke 13:33). The telling was one of those things ‘told to them in darkness, but which they were afterward to speak in the light’; and it was told to the Twelve because they ‘would be more immediately exposed to peril with him,’ so that ‘being fore-warned, they might be fore-armed.’ Henry then gives two reasons it was unfit for the crowd, and they pull in opposite directions: those ‘cool toward him’ would have been driven to ‘turn their backs upon him,’ frightened off by the scandal of the cross; those ‘hot for him’ would have been driven ‘to take up arms in his defense,’ occasioning an uproar — and such methods are ‘utterly disagreeable to the genius of his kingdom, which is not of this world.’ He notices even where the words were spoken: not in synagogue or house but ‘in the way, as they travelled along,’ which teaches us to keep such talk up on our own journeys. That Christ returned to the subject so often shows ‘his heart was upon his suffering-work’: it filled him ‘not with fear, then he would have studied to avoid it… but with desire and expectation.’ And so, Henry adds, ‘it is good for us to be often thinking and speaking of our death’ — one way of dying daily.
18:
‘Behold, we go up to Jerusalem; and the Son of man shall be betrayed unto the chief priests and scribes, and they shall condemn him to death.’ The precision of the prophecy, and the willingness it reveals, are what the commentators press.

The grammatical-historical commentators detail the prediction. Barnes lays out the stages: betrayed (Matthew 26:15), condemned by a Sanhedrin that lacked power to execute (Matthew 26:66), and so delivered to the Gentiles — all foretold in Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9:26. Ellicott notes the new definiteness over Matthew 17:22: Jerusalem the scene, the chief priests and scribes the actors, the Gentiles their instruments, with the mocking, spitting and scourging now ‘new elements’ brought ‘vividly… before His mind and theirs.’

The Reformed Calvin draws the doctrine: Christ ‘was endued with divine fortitude for overcoming the terrors of death, for he knowingly and willingly hastens to undergo it,’ and the minute detail of the circumstances is itself ‘a still more evident proof of his Divinity,’ for none but God could so foresee them. Yet he does not spare the disciples the ‘very grievous offense’ of seeing the whole sacred order opposed to Christ, but candidly declares it and points to his resurrection as the way to overcome the temptation.

Cyril of Jerusalem presses the willingness to its reason: Christ ‘came to His passion willingly… lest the whole world should perish in its sins,’ and therefore ‘the Cross is a glory to Jesus.’

The Puritan Henry measures the same courage against ordinary human nerve. The things foretold here — condemnation, delivery to the Gentiles, mocking, scourging, crucifixion — are ‘frightful things, and the certain foresight of them was enough to damp an ordinary resolution’; yet, as was foretold of him, ‘he did not fail, nor was discouraged’ (Isaiah 42:4). Henry puts the paradox in a sentence: ‘the more clearly he foresaw his sufferings, the more cheerfully he went forth to meet them.’ So the foreknowledge and the willingness are not two facts here but one. A death foretold in every particular — the betrayal, the unjust condemnation by a court without power to kill, the handing over to Gentile hands — is embraced by the one who alone could have seen it coming; and the same breath that declares the offence points the disciples past it.
19:
‘And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him: and the third day he shall rise again.’ The Gentile instruments, the manner of the death, and a resurrection the disciples could not grasp are the three things here.

The grammatical-historical commentators identify the agents and the prophecies. Gill and Clarke specify that the delivery to the Gentiles meant Pilate and the Roman soldiers — the mocking by Herod and his soldiers (Luke 23:11), the scourging and crucifixion by Pilate — crucifixion being a Roman, not a Jewish, punishment. Barnes ties the scourging to Isaiah 53:5 and the delivery to Acts 3:13. Robertson observes that ‘the details fall on deaf ears, even the point of the resurrection.’ Clarke marvels that they were unwittingly offering ‘that sacrifice which was to make an atonement… for the whole world,’ and adds that the wrath of man would only praise God (compare Psalms 76:10).

Ellicott dwells on the resurrection clause: it ‘came as a sequel… The Master looked beyond the suffering to the victory over death, but the disciples could not enter into the meaning,’ for, as Luke reports (Luke 18:34), ‘they understood none of these things… this saying was hid from them.’ All was to them ‘a dark and dim dream.’

The Puritan Henry supplies the reason the two nations appear together: ‘Christ suffered from the malice both of Jews and Gentiles, because he was to suffer for the salvation both of Jews and Gentiles; both had a hand in his death, because he was to reconcile both by his cross’ (Ephesians 2:16). On the last clause he asks why Christ keeps joining it to the rest, and gives three answers. First, for himself: ‘he endured the cross for the joy set before him; he foresaw he should rise again, and rise quickly, the third day,’ so that ‘the reward is not only sure, but very near’ (compare John 13:32). Second, for the disciples, ‘who would be overwhelmed and greatly terrified by his sufferings.’ Third, for us, ‘to direct us, under all the sufferings of this present time, to keep up a believing prospect of the glory to be revealed… which will enable us to call the present afflictions light, and but for a moment.’ The clause the disciples could not hear was therefore spoken as much for later readers as for them.
20:
The mother of Zebedee’s sons comes worshipping, to ask a favour. Coming just after the passion prediction, the request betrays an earthly view of the kingdom; whether the mother or the sons were the true petitioners is disputed.

The grammatical-historical commentators set the scene. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson identify the mother as Salome (Matthew 27:56, Mark 15:40), possibly a sister of the Lord’s mother (John 19:25), prompting her sons because of the kinship. Robertson calls the timing ‘surely an inopportune’ one, their minds preoccupied with the twelve thrones of Matthew 19:28. Ellicott notes she shared the hope that ‘the kingdom of God should immediately appear’ (Luke 19:11).

The Latin and Greek fathers moralise. Jerome blames her ‘womanish eagerness’ that grasps the present and forgets the future. Pseudo-Chrysostom praises Salome as ‘truly peaceful’ and her sons as seeking ‘not earthly things, but heavenly,’ yet faults the request as ‘inconsiderate,’ and reads ‘Ye know not what ye ask’ as a rebuke of ignorance, not malice. Origen sees ‘womanish simplicity’ and the brothers’ imperfect notions of the kingdom. Augustine harmonises with Mark, where the sons themselves ask (Mark 10:35).

The Reformed Calvin calls the narrative ‘a bright mirror of human vanity,’ showing how ‘holy zeal is often accompanied by ambition’; the brothers, restrained by bashfulness, put their mother forward, their conscience reproving them.

The Puritan Henry agrees that the sons set her on, and reads the manoeuvre as a symptom: ‘though proud people think well of themselves, they would not be thought to do so, and therefore affect nothing more than a show of humility’ (compare Colossians 2:18), getting others ‘put on to court that honour for them, which they are ashamed to court for themselves’ — as Adonijah set Bathsheba to speak for him. It was Salome’s ‘weakness thus to become the tool of their ambition, which she should have given a check to.’ Henry also explains the timing the others only wonder at: it was probably the last word of the foregoing discourse, ‘that the third day he should rise again,’ which prompted them. ‘They concluded that his resurrection would be his entrance upon his kingdom, and therefore were resolved to put in betimes for the best place.’ What was said to comfort them ‘they thus abused, and were puffed up with’ — ‘as sweetmeats in a foul stomach produce bile.’ That Christ bore with it at all is, for Henry, of a piece with his way: ‘whom Christ loves best he reproves most.’
21:
‘Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the left, in thy kingdom.’ The request mingles a true faith in Christ’s reign with a carnal mistake about its nature.

The grammatical-historical commentators expose the error. Barnes says they were ‘still looking for a temporal kingdom’ with ‘pomp and glory,’ seeking the places of highest honour at a prince’s right and left (1 Kings 2:19). Clarke connects the request with the promise of the twelve thrones (Matthew 19:28) taken literally, and notes the rabbinic arrangement of the Sanhedrin’s president flanked by the ‘father’ and the ‘sage,’ suggesting they sought ecclesiastical rather than secular honours. Ellicott observes the favour already shown — John ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’ (John 13:23), James one of the chosen three — might have seemed to warrant the petition.

The Reformed Calvin balances praise and blame: it was ‘a noble specimen of faith’ to expect a kingdom when Christ appeared ‘under the mean aspect of a servant’; yet ‘how easily the pure seed… becomes degenerate,’ for they imagined a kingdom that ‘had no existence’ and coveted the highest places. He draws the prayer that God would keep our faith ‘pure from all mixture.’ Gill notes Christ’s humanity, goodness and patience in not upbraiding their pride. The Wesleyan Wesley adds tersely that ‘still they expected a temporal kingdom.’

The Puritan Henry weighs the two elements as finely as Calvin does, and then presses the petition’s shape. ‘It was a great degree of faith, that they were confident of his kingdom, though now he appeared in meanness; but a great degree of ignorance, that they still expected a temporal kingdom… when Christ had so often told them of sufferings and self-denial.’ Note what they asked for: ‘they ask not for employment in this kingdom, but for honour only; and no place would serve them… but the highest, next to Christ, and above every body else.’ Henry marks even the tactic of the opening request — to ask first ‘for a general grant, that he would do a certain thing for them, not in faith, but in presumption,’ leaning on the promise ‘Ask, and it shall be given you’ without its implied condition. Then he distinguishes the ambitions: ‘it is a holy ambition to strive to excel others in grace and holiness; but it is a sinful ambition to covet to exceed others in pomp and grandeur.’ And he turns on the petitioners the prophet’s word: ‘seekest thou great things for thyself, when thou hast just now heard of thy Master’s being mocked, and scourged, and crucified? For shame! Seek them not’ (Jeremiah 45:5).
22:
‘Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of?’ The cup, and the washing joined to it, stand for suffering and martyrdom, and the brothers’ confident ‘We are able’ betrays their ignorance.

The grammatical-historical commentators expound the imagery and the text. Barnes and Ellicott show that ‘to drink of a cup’ means to be afflicted (Isaiah 51:17, Psalms 75:8), and the baptism to be overwhelmed in floods of calamity (Psalms 42:7, Luke 12:50). Lightfoot notes that the Jewish rite, a total plunging, fitly signified ‘the most cruel kind of death.’ Clarke and Ellicott both observe that the second clause is absent from many of the best manuscripts, probably borrowed from Mark. Robertson parses ‘ask’ as an indirect middle — ‘a selfish request’ — and calls their answer an ‘amazing proof of their ignorance… they had not caught the martyr spirit.’

The Reformed Calvin holds that Christ ‘corrects their ambition… by holding out the cross,’ teaching that none will share his kingdom ‘who has not previously shared in his sufferings and death’; their bold reply ‘manifests the presumption of the flesh.’ The Wesleyan Clarke turns it on those who covet church office, and Wesley says all who share that kingdom ‘must first share in his sufferings.’ Cyril of Jerusalem names martyrdom itself a baptism ‘in their own blood.’

The Puritan Henry locates the ignorance in the road rather than the goal: ‘they know not what they ask, who ask for the end, but overlook the means.’ These men ‘imagined their warfare was accomplished when it was scarcely begun, and they had yet but run with the footmen’; they ‘dream of being in Canaan presently, and consider not what they shall do in the swellings of Jordan.’ Hence his maxim: ‘we are all apt, when we are but girding on the harness, to boast as though we had put it off’ — praying ‘for the glory of wearing the crown,’ and not ‘for grace to bear the cross in our way to it.’ Yet Henry will not leave the figure a terror. ‘It is but a cup, not an ocean… bitter perhaps, but we shall see the bottom of it; it is a cup in the hand of a Father’ (John 18:11); and if a man be dipped, ‘that is the worst of it, not drowned; perplexed, but not in despair.’ So each reader must put the question to himself, since ‘religion, if it be worth any thing, is worth every thing; but it is worth little, if it be not worth suffering for.’
23:
‘Ye shall drink indeed of my cup… but to sit on my right hand… is not mine to give, but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared of my Father.’ A martyrdom is predicted, and a misleading translation corrected.

The grammatical-historical commentators press both points. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all object that the italicised words ‘it shall be given’ pervert the sense, making Christ deny that he bestows rewards — contrary to John 5:22; the true rendering is ‘is not mine to give, except to those for whom it is prepared of my Father’ (the same phrase recurs in Matthew 25:34). As prediction, they note the contrast in the brothers’ fates: James the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2), John surviving to old age, exile, and the struggle of Revelation 1:9.

The Reformed Calvin explains that Christ ‘surrenders nothing,’ but states that the Father had not assigned to him ‘this office of appointing to each person his own peculiar place’; he reasons not about his power but about his calling, and warns us ‘to be wise with sobriety’ and not pry into the future state (1 John 3:2). The Wesleyan Wesley agrees the place ‘is his to give in the strictest propriety,’ but only for those prepared, whom he describes as the men ‘who endure to the end in the faith that worketh by love.’

The Puritan Henry arrives independently at that same corrective reading, and adds a moral edge the others miss: the chief seats fall not ‘to those that seek and are ambitious of it, but to those that by great humility and self-denial are prepared for it.’ Why the silence about who they are? Because ‘the infirmity of their present state could not bear such a discovery with any evenness’; and besides, ‘the lowest seat in heaven is an abundant recompence for the greatest sufferings on earth.’ Degrees of honour above he thinks probable, but holds them, like the blessedness itself, ‘purposed and prepared in the eternal counsel of God.’ On the cup he turns the prediction into comfort: ‘sufferings foreseen will be the more easily borne,’ for ‘Christ began in suffering for us, and expects we should pledge him in suffering for him’ — he ‘will have us know the worst, that we may make the best of our way to heaven.’ As for John, Henry notes he ‘died in his bed,’ yet drank often of the bitter cup: banished to Patmos, and, if the historians may be credited, at Ephesus ‘put into a caldron of boiling oil, but was miraculously preserved.’
24:
‘And when the ten heard it, they were moved with indignation against the two brethren.’ What moved the ten was itself a symptom of the fault they resented, not a righteous zeal.

The grammatical-historical commentators name the fault. Barnes and Robertson note the strong word for ‘angry resentment’: the ten ‘felt that James and John had taken advantage of their relation to Jesus.’ Ellicott is explicit that it was ‘not a righteous indignation… but rather the jealousy of rivals,’ angry that the two had sought an unfair advantage. Clarke generalises that ‘the ambition which leads to spiritual lordship… has proved the ruin of the most flourishing Churches.’

The Greek and Latin fathers probe the motives. Chrysostom observes that only now, hearing the Lord rebuke the two, did the others vent the grief they had nursed since the Transfiguration, not daring before ‘out of respect to their teacher.’ Pseudo-Chrysostom remarks that ‘as the two had asked carnally, so now the ten are grieved carnally,’ for ‘to have another above us is mortifying to our vanity.’ Origen notes the rulers of this world are ‘severe and oppressive,’ but among Christ’s own it shall not be so.

The Reformed Calvin judges the ten’s displeasure ‘far from being well-founded’: the Lord intended to ‘lay open a disease which was lurking within them,’ for ‘there was not one… who would willingly yield to others.’

The Puritan Henry draws a fine distinction the others leave implicit. The ten were vexed not that the brothers wanted preferment — that they wanted themselves — but that the two wanted to be preferred before them, ‘which was a reflection upon them.’ Most displeasure at wrongdoing, he says, runs that way: ‘it is not because it is sin, but because it touches them. They will inform against a man that swears; but it is only if he swear at them, and affront them, not because he dishonours God.’ The ten resented the two ‘though they themselves, nay because they themselves, were as ambitious’ — it being usual to resent ‘those sins in others which they allow of and indulge in themselves.’ Then the observation that holds the whole scene together: ‘nothing makes more mischief among brethren… than ambition, and desire of greatness. We never find Christ’s disciples quarreling, but something of this was at the bottom of it.’ The quarrel therefore exposes a disease common to the whole company, which is why the words on servanthood that follow (vv.26–28) are addressed not to two offenders but to twelve.
25:
‘The princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them… but it shall not be so among you.’ Christ sets the world’s way of lordship against the servanthood of his kingdom, and the commentators differ over how far the prohibition reaches.

The grammatical-historical commentators draw the contrast. Barnes says the kings of the earth raise favourites to power, ‘but my kingdom is established in a different manner… no ranks; no places of dominion,’ the most distinguished being the most humble; he glosses ‘minister’ as deacon, a servant. Clarke and Ellicott render the two strong verbs ‘lord it over’ and exercise oppressive authority (compare 1 Peter 5:3), Clarke adding that when ‘political matters are brought into the Church… both are ruined.’

The Reformed Calvin distinguishes ‘the spiritual government of his Church’ from ‘the empires of the world’: pastors are appointed ‘not to rule but to serve.’ But he guards the civil office carefully, against the Anabaptist error of shutting magistrates out of the Church — the comparison is ‘not between Christians and ungodly men, but between the nature of their offices’ — and though even kings ‘do not rule justly… unless they serve,’ their office, unlike the apostolic, admits scepter and throne. Gill likewise limits the saying to apostles and pastors, who have no ‘lordly power’ over one another. The Wesleyan Wesley puts it tersely: the disciples imagined the chief in his kingdom would lord it as the Gentiles do, ‘but it will be quite otherwise.’

The Puritan Henry takes the ban further than any of them. He first paints the princes: they ‘would bear sway, would carry all before them, have every body truckle to them, and every sheaf bow to theirs,’ having it cried before them ‘Bow the knee’ like Nebuchadnezzar, ‘who slew, and kept alive, at pleasure.’ Against that he sets his epigram: ‘principality doth no more become ministers than Gentilism doth Christians.’ And then the stroke that parts him from Calvin: the saying forbids ‘not only tyranny, and abuse of power, but the claim or use of any such secular authority as the princes of the Gentiles lawfully exercise.’ His reason is not that such power is wrong in itself but that it is unsafe in any hands: ‘so hard is it for vain men, even good men, to have such authority, and not to be puffed up with it, and do more hurt than good with it, that our Lord Jesus saw fit wholly to banish it out of his church.’ He cites Paul disowning ‘dominion over the faith of any’ (2 Corinthians 1:24), and adds the point that turns the rebuke back on the quarrel: if no such power was ever to exist in the church, ‘it was nonsense for them to be striving who should have it.’
26:
‘Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.’ Christ does not condemn the desire for greatness but redirects it to service.

The grammatical-historical commentators draw the paradox. Robertson is emphatic that ‘Jesus does not condemn the desire to become great… a laudable ambition’; there are ‘great ones’ among Christians, but they do not ‘lord it over’ others — ‘the way to be first… is to be your servant… a complete reversal of popular opinion.’ Ellicott urges the ambitious disciple ‘at once to satisfy and purify’ his longing ‘by finding his greatness in active service,’ for that service ‘is in itself the truest and highest greatness.’ Barnes points to the deacon’s servant-office (compare Matthew 23:11).

The Reformed Calvin explains that since ‘every man is carried away by a love of himself,’ Christ bids that passion be turned to a new object: ‘let the only greatness… you desire be to submit to your brethren.’ The Wesleyan Clarke draws a fivefold portrait of the true minister — not lording over the flock, not imperious, reforming the weak by loving instruction, serving with all his talents, ready to lay down his life. Gill restrains the saying from abolishing all church order, applying it to the equality of the apostles and pastors among themselves.

The Puritan Henry makes the duty concrete before he makes it honourable. The followers of Christ ‘must be ready to stoop to the meanest offices of love for the good one of another,’ serving one another ‘for mutual edification’ — which, he says, ‘includes both humility and usefulness.’ Then the dignity: those to be ‘best accounted of, and most respected, in the church’ are ‘not those that are dignified with high and mighty names, like the names of the great ones of the earth, that appear in pomp,’ but those ‘most humble and self-denying,’ who ‘lay out themselves most to do good, though to the diminishing of themselves.’ Such ‘honour God most, and those he will honour.’ Henry fixes the whole reversal in a single comparison: ‘as he must become a fool that would be wise, so he must become a servant that would be chief.’ The disciple’s ambition, in other words, is not killed but inverted: it is told where to climb by being told how far to stoop.
27:
‘And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.’ The saying intensifies the one before it: the higher the place desired, the lower the service required.

The grammatical-historical commentators mark the deepening. Ellicott notes that ‘servant’ (better, slave) ‘implies a lower and more menial service’ than the ‘minister’ of v.26, just as ‘chief’ or ‘first’ is higher than ‘great’; he warns against the ‘false antithesis’ that would assign service to this life and greatness to the next — ‘the greatness is the service.’ Gill glosses ‘chief’ as wishing the first place, the pre-eminence in the Messiah’s kingdom.

The Wesleyan Clarke draws from ‘servant’ — the lowest secular office, often a slave — a portrait of the gospel minister: he is not to consider himself a lord over Christ’s flock, not to act with an imperious spirit, to reform the weak by loving instruction rather than censure, to count apostolic greatness as serving the followers of Christ with all his powers, and to be ready, if required, to lay down his life for their salvation.

The Puritan Henry supplies a candidate. ‘St. Paul was a great example of this; he laboured more abundantly than they all, made himself (as some would call it) a drudge to his work; and is not he chief? Do we not by consent call him the great apostle, though he called himself less than the least?’ Henry then ventures further than any of the others dare. Perhaps the Lord ‘had an eye to him’ in saying there were last that should be first, Paul being ‘born out of due time’ (1 Corinthians 15:8), ‘not only the youngest child of the family of the apostles, but a posthumous one, yet he became greatest.’ And perhaps — the conjecture is startling — ‘he it was for whom the first post of honour in Christ’s kingdom was reserved and prepared of his Father, not for James who sought it’; so that just as Paul rose, ‘Providence ordered it so that James was cut off’ (Acts 12:2), ‘that in the college of the twelve Paul might be substituted in his room.’ Whether or not the guess holds, it fastens the chapter together: the place the brothers asked for was prepared, and prepared for the man who never asked.
28:
‘Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.’ Here is the ground of the whole call to service, and the chapter’s clearest statement of substitutionary atonement.

The grammatical-historical commentators expound the ransom. Barnes defines it as ‘a price paid for the redemption of captives’: men are captives to sin (Romans 3:9-20), and Christ ‘died in the place of sinners,’ God accepting his death ‘in the place of the eternal suffering of the redeemed’ (1 Peter 1:18-19). Clarke and Ellicott root lutron in the Septuagint’s ransom-price (Exodus 21:30, Leviticus 25:50), Clarke rendering ‘a ransom instead of many’ and noting the whole ancient world believed in vicarious sacrifice. Robertson, against those who would evade it, insists Jesus ‘rises to the full consciousness of the significance of his death,’ the preposition anti carrying ‘the notion of exchange’ — the purchase-money for manumitting slaves.

The Reformed Calvin confirms the doctrine: Christ ‘voluntarily emptied himself’ (Philippians 2:7), and ‘his life is the price of our redemption,’ this single word overturning the ‘idle talk of the Papists’ about merit. He reads ‘many’ not as a fixed number but in contrast to one — Christ set against ‘all the rest of men’ (compare Romans 5:15, 1 Timothy 2:6). Cyril of Jerusalem hears behind the title the Son of man of Daniel’s vision (Daniel 7:13).

The Puritan Henry presses the first clause closer than the rest, with a distinction that saves it from contradicting the Gospels. Christ was ‘indeed ministered to as a poor man… there were those that ministered to him of their substance’ (Luke 8:2-3); ‘but he was never ministered to as a great man; he never took state upon him, was not waited on at table; he once washed his disciples’ feet, but we never read that they washed his feet.’ He had ‘no pompous train of state-servants to attend him,’ and instead ‘made himself a servant to the sick and diseased; was as ready to their requests as ever any servant was at the beck of his master.’ On the ransom Henry sets the princes of v.25 against their Lord: they ‘make the lives of many a ransom for their own honour,’ whereas Christ ‘gives his honour and life too’ for his subjects, whose blood is precious to him (compare Psalms 72:14). And where Calvin takes ‘many’ as the contrast to one, Henry turns it pastorally: it was ‘sufficient for all, effectual for many; and, if for many, then, saith the poor doubting soul, Why not for me?’
29:
As Jesus departs from Jericho, a great multitude follows and two blind men cry out. The commentators divide on harmonising the accounts, but unite on the beggars’ persevering faith.

The grammatical-historical commentators tackle the harmony. Barnes and Robertson reconcile Mark’s and Luke’s naming of one man (Bartimaeus) with Matthew’s two — the one being better known — and Luke’s placing the miracle as Jesus ‘came nigh’ Jericho (Luke 18:35), Robertson suggesting old and new Jericho with the men ‘between the two towns.’ Barnes gives a full account of Jericho’s history (Joshua 6:26, 1 Kings 16:34).

The Greek and Latin fathers read both the persistence and the figure. Pseudo-Chrysostom marvels that ‘spiritual love feels no fatigue’ and that the blind, having ‘nothing free about them but their voice… pursued Him with their voice’; ‘faith is quickened by being prohibited.’ Chrysostom notes Christ ‘suffered them to be forbidden, that their desire might be the more evidenced.’ Origen and Augustine allegorise the two as Israel and the Gentiles, or as souls coming by faith to be enlightened, who must cry over the din of the worldly crowd — for ‘bad or lukewarm Christians are a hindrance to good Christians.’ Jerome and Raban take the men for the Pharisees and Sadducees, or read Jericho (‘the moon’) as the changeful world.

The Puritan Henry works the circumstances for their lessons. That two cried together is itself commended, for ‘joint-prayer is pleasing to Christ’ (Matthew 18:19): ‘these joint-sufferers were joint-suitors; being companions in the same tribulation, they were partners in the same supplication,’ and fellow-sufferers do well to pray together, each quickening the other’s fervency. That they sat by the way-side teaches those who would have mercy to ‘place themselves there where his out-goings are’ — ‘it is good thus to way-lay Christ, to be in his road.’ That they only heard him pass is turned to account too: ‘though they were blind, they were not deaf. Seeing and hearing are the learning senses,’ and where one is wanting the other is often sharpened. And that they cried at once, asking no questions ‘who were with him, or whether he was in haste,’ was wisdom, for the opportunity, ‘if once let slip, it may never return’ — ‘we do not find that Christ ever came to Jericho again.’ Henry even reads the crowd: it followed ‘for loaves, and some for love, some for curiosity, and some in expectation of his temporal reign… very few with desire to be taught their duty’; yet for those few the miracles were worked in public, so that the rest, unconvinced, would be ‘the more inexcusable.’
30:
‘Two blind men… cried out, Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou Son of David.’ The harmonising question returns, and with it the faith expressed in the title ‘Son of David.’

The grammatical-historical commentators address the number. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson again explain that Mark and Luke mention only the conspicuous Bartimaeus; Gill proposes ‘three blind men’ (one before, two after Jericho); Ellicott candidly allows that Luke, inquiring on the spot, ‘may have made his narrative more accurate.’ They note the men echoed the crowd’s whispered identification, using, like the woman of Canaan (Matthew 15:22), the most popular messianic title and appealing ‘to the pity of the King.’ The Wesleyan Wesley adds that Bartimaeus was ‘far the more eminent… and spoke for both.’

The Reformed Calvin and the Alexandrian Origen weigh the confession. Calvin says they ‘confer on Christ no ordinary honor’ in seeking relief from him, and their faith ‘is still more clearly exhibited’ in acknowledging him Messiah, the ‘Son of David’ — not ‘some Prophet,’ but the ‘only Author of salvation.’ Origen gathers the various titles given Christ — ‘Son of David’ by these and the Canaanite, ‘Son of God’ by others, with or without the ‘truly’ (v.33) — to show ‘the difference of those who come’ to him.

The Puritan Henry takes the short cry apart as a model of prayer and finds four things in it. Importunity: they ‘cried out as men in earnest; men in want are earnest, of course. Cold desires do but beg denials.’ Humility: in asking mercy they do not specify the favour ‘or prescribing what, much less pleading merit’ — ‘they ask not for silver and gold, though they were poor, but mercy, mercy.’ Faith: the title is itself a plea, confessing him Lord, and so one ‘who had authority to command deliverance for them’ — indeed ‘it was by the Holy Ghost that they called Christ Lord’ (1 Corinthians 12:3). And in naming him Son of David they lean on his goodness ‘as Messiah, of whom so many kind and tender things had been foretold, particularly his compassion to the poor and needy’ (compare Psalms 72:12-13). It is therefore ‘of excellent use, in prayer, to eye Christ in the grace and glory of his Messiahship; to remember that he is the Son of David, whose office it is to help, and save, and to plead it with him.’ The fourth thing, perseverance, the next verse will supply.
31:
‘The multitude rebuked them… but they cried the more.’ The rebuke only intensified the blind men’s faith, and the commentators draw from it a lesson on perseverance in prayer.

The grammatical-historical commentators describe the rebuke. Gill suggests the multitude, whether friends or enemies, chid them as troublesome or were displeased at the ‘high characters’ — Lord, Son of David — they gave Christ. Barnes adds from Mark that Jesus stood still and ordered them called, and that Bartimaeus ‘cast away his garment’ in haste to come. Ellicott observes the litanies of Christendom have for centuries been ‘modelled on the Kyrie Eleïson’ that came from their lips.

The Wesleyan Clarke turns it to the soul: ‘whenever a soul begins to cry after Jesus… the world and the devil join together to drown its cries’; let such ‘cry a great deal the more,’ for the rebuke is ‘a proof that the salvation of God is nigh.’ Wesley likewise: those who begin to cry after the Son of David will be charged to hold their peace, but ‘let those who feel their need of him cry the more; otherwise they will come short of a cure.’

The Reformed Calvin finds it ‘surprising that the disciples of Christ… should wish to drive wretched men from the favor of Christ,’ and warns that often ‘the greater part of those who profess the name of Christ… rather hinder or delay our approach’; perseverance is therefore necessary, the redoubled cry overcoming every obstacle Satan throws in the way.

The Puritan Henry supplies the mechanics of the thing, and a hard observation besides. Hindrance is to be reckoned on: in following Christ with our prayers ‘we must expect to meet with hindrances and manifold discouragements from within and from without, something or other that bids us hold our peace’ — and such rebukes ‘are permitted, that faith and fervency, patience and perseverance, may be tried.’ Who gives them is the hard part: ‘the sincere and serious beggars at Christ’s door commonly meet with the worst rebukes from those that follow him but in pretence and hypocrisy.’ As for the effect, Henry has the best image of it: ‘the stream of fervency, if it be stopped, will rise and swell the higher.’ The striving is not wasted either, for ‘the more it is striven for, the more it will be prized and thankfully acknowledged.’ When they were in pursuit of such a mercy ‘it was no time to compliment,’ and so men ‘ought always to pray, and not to faint’ (Luke 18:1).
32:
‘And Jesus stood still, and called them, and said, What will ye that I shall do unto you?’ The stopping, and the asking of what he already knew, are what the commentators dwell on.

The grammatical-historical commentators note the manner. Gill says the standing still ‘shows the strength of faith, the force of prayer, and the great regard Christ has to both.’ Ellicott gives, from Mark, the very message — ‘Be of good cheer, arise; He calleth thee’ — and Bartimaeus flinging off his cloak to leap up and come; the question is asked ‘with the clear insight of sympathy.’ Clarke exclaims that ‘the cry of a believing penitent… is sufficient to stop the most merciful Jesus,’ for one immortal soul outweighs all the irrational creation.

The Reformed Calvin explains why Christ asks a seemingly needless question: ‘he had determined to grant their requests,’ and there is no doubt ‘they prayed by a special movement of the Holy Spirit,’ for God does not permit all simply to pray for bodily healing; a rule is prescribed ‘what we ought to ask,’ from which we depart only when the Spirit suggests a special prayer. Christ puts the question ‘for the sake of all the people,’ to awaken the crowd to observe the miracle.

The Puritan Henry weighs the halt against the errand. Christ ‘was now going up to Jerusalem, and was straitened till his work there was accomplished; and yet he stood still to cure these blind men’ — from which, ‘when we are ever so much in haste about any business, yet we should be willing to stand still to do good.’ The summons was no necessity but a courtesy: he called them ‘not because he could not cure them at a distance, but because he would do it in the most obliging and instructive way, and would countenance weak but willing patients and petitioners.’ Christ, says Henry, ‘not only enjoins us to pray, but invites us; holds out the golden sceptre to us, and bids us come touch the top of it.’ As for the question, he reads it as a fair offer with one easy condition, since Christ ‘would know it from them, whether they begged only for alms, as from a common person, or for a cure, as from the Messiah.’ Prayer, on this account, is not for God’s information but for ours: ‘the waterman in the boat, who with his hook takes hold of the shore, does not thereby pull the shore to the boat, but the boat to the shore. So in prayer we do not draw the mercy to ourselves, but ourselves to the mercy.’
33:
‘They say unto him, Lord, that our eyes may be opened.’ The definiteness of the request, and the faith behind it, are the points here.

The grammatical-historical commentators note the plain petition. Barnes and Clarke observe that the blind men ask not for alms but for sight: ‘a hungry man can easily ask bread… the afflicted heart alone can tell its own sorrows.’ Ellicott records that Mark preserves the Hebrew word actually uttered, Rabboni (compare John 20:16), a title of deep reverence.

The Reformed Gill draws out the faith: that they asked for the recovery of sight, not alms, shows they ‘made no doubt’ of Christ’s power, and the opening of blind eyes was prophesied as a work of the Messiah (Isaiah 35:5) — a prophecy that may have ‘encouraged their faith to expect a cure from him.’ They sought sight so that they might ‘get their bread in another way,’ not choosing, like idle beggars, to remain under their calamity.

The Puritan Henry marks how readily such a petition comes, and turns the ease of it into a reproach. This was a request ‘such a one as they never made to any one else’; and no wonder, for ‘the wants and burthens of the body we are soon sensible of, and can readily relate’ — ubi dolor, ubi digitus, the finger goes promptly to the seat of the pain. The contrast is with the other blindness: ‘O that we were but as apprehensive of our spiritual maladies, and could as feelingly complain of them, especially our spiritual blindness!’ The difficulty, Henry says, is that the complaint is not felt, for ‘many are spiritually blind, and yet say they see’ (John 9:41). Were a man once sensible of his darkness, he ‘should soon apply’ himself to the one ‘who alone has the eye-salve,’ with the beggars’ own words in his mouth. So the two petitions sit side by side in Henry’s reading: the one these men made, definite and reverent and granted within the minute; and the one most men never make, because they do not know they need it.
34:
‘So Jesus had compassion on them, and touched their eyes: and immediately they received sight, and they followed him.’ Pity, power, and the discipleship that crowned them are all remarked on.

The grammatical-historical commentators stress pity and proof. Clarke and Robertson note the verb of tender compassion (the ‘bowels’ of mercy) and that the touch of Christ’s hand ‘would sooth the eyes as they were healed.’ Barnes adds from Mark and Luke the word ‘Thy faith hath saved thee’: faith ‘had no power to open the eyes, but it led them to Jesus,’ and he marshals the marks of an undoubted cure — the men well known, strangers to Jesus, healed before deeply interested multitudes who ‘could easily have detected the imposition.’ Ellicott observes that compassion, not the popular demand for signs, drew out the work.

The Reformed Calvin reads the following as ‘an expression of gratitude’: the healed men became disciples, presenting themselves ‘as mirrors of the grace of Christ’ and so confirming the certainty of the miracle. Gill marks that the pity was shown ‘by some outward sign.’ The Wesleyan Clarke draws the appeal: ‘whosoever thou art, act in behalf of thy soul as these blind men did in behalf of their sight… he is passing by, and thou art passing into eternity.’

The Puritan Henry divides the verse between the pity and the power, and then takes up the last clause. ‘Misery is the object of mercy,’ and it was the tender mercy of God that ‘gave light and sight to them that sat in darkness’ (Luke 1:78-79); such calamities we cannot relieve as he did, ‘but we may and must pity them… and draw out our soul to them.’ For the power, he asks and answers in one breath: ‘he that formed the eye, can he not heal it? Yes, he can, he did, he did it easily… he did it effectually’ — which showed not merely that he was sent of God but ‘on what errand he was sent—to give sight to those that are spiritually blind, to turn them from darkness to light.’ On the following Henry supplies the sentence the chapter ends with: ‘none follow Christ blindfold. He first by his grace opens men’s eyes, and so draws their hearts after him.’ Hence his rule: ‘the best evidence of spiritual illumination is a constant inseparable adherence to Jesus Christ as our Lord and Leader.’
